title: Unify gameplay on a single reusable multiplication board with mode-driven cell behavior
body:
This change centers the app on one permanent multiplication grid for all activities, with game modes only changing cell state/content instead of swapping layouts. It also adds mobile-first layout control so the grid resizes between a fixed header and collapsible bottom panel.

- **Core board architecture**
  - Added `GridCell` as the reusable cell primitive with explicit state flags: `Active`, `Disabled`, `Placeholder`, `Selected`, `Highlighted`, `CorrectAnswer`, `IncorrectAnswer`, `Header`.
  - Added `GridManager` to generate/own the full table (including header row/column and top-left empty corner), maintain references, and expose state/value APIs.
  - Grid structure remains constant; unused positions are represented as placeholder/disabled cells, not removed.

- **Game mode separation**
  - Added `GameModeBase` with a standard lifecycle/interface (`Initialize`, `Activate`, `Deactivate`, cell click handling).
  - Implemented mode classes that reconfigure the shared board only:
    - `RandomAnswerMode`
    - `FillMissingCellsMode` (unique hidden-cell selection)
    - `RowPracticeMode`
    - `ColumnPracticeMode`
    - `FactorFinderMode`
    - `TimedChallengeMode`
  - Added `GameModeController` to switch modes against one `GridManager` instance (with default index clamping).

- **Mobile layout behavior**
  - Added `MobileBoardLayoutController` for the required 3-zone structure:
    - fixed top header
    - center grid area
    - collapsible slide-up bottom menu
  - Recomputes available grid height on menu toggle/dimension changes and resizes cell dimensions from available space (not fixed pixels).

- **Documentation**
  - Updated `README.md` to describe the shared-grid architecture and script responsibilities.

```csharp
// Shared board, mode-specific behavior
public abstract class GameModeBase : MonoBehaviour
{
    protected GridManager GridManager;

    public virtual void Activate()
    {
        GridManager.CellPressed += HandleCellPressed;
        ConfigureMode(); // mode only mutates states/labels on existing cells
    }

    protected abstract void ConfigureMode();
}
```

<details>

<summary>Original prompt</summary>

The core design of the application should revolve around a single reusable multiplication grid system that serves as the foundation for every game mode in the app. Rather than creating separate screens or layouts for each activity, the application should always display the same grid structure and allow different game modes to populate and interact with that grid in different ways. This keeps development simpler, ensures a consistent user experience, and makes it easy to add new learning activities in the future without rebuilding the interface.

The application is intended for Unity 2D Mobile and should be designed with touch controls as the primary interaction method. The screen should be divided into three major areas. At the top of the screen should be a fixed header bar containing game selection controls, current score, streak information, player progress, and access to settings. The center portion of the screen should be dedicated almost entirely to the multiplication grid, as this is the primary learning and interaction area. At the bottom of the screen should be a slide-up menu panel that can be expanded or collapsed by the player. This menu will contain options such as game mode selection, difficulty settings, number ranges, practice targets, and buttons for starting, resetting, or changing activities.

The multiplication grid itself should be treated as a permanent board rather than a game-specific interface. Every cell position should always exist, even if a particular game mode does not use that position. If a game mode only requires a portion of the board, unused cells should be populated with placeholder elements rather than removed entirely. This ensures that the grid remains properly aligned, maintains consistent sizing, and avoids layout issues on different device sizes and screen resolutions.

The recommended structure is a traditional multiplication table. The top-left corner cell remains empty. The top row contains column header values, while the leftmost column contains row header values. All remaining cells represent multiplication values derived from their row and column headers. For example, if practicing multiplication tables from 1 through 10, the board would contain header rows and columns plus the multiplication cells themselves. Every position should be represented by a button-based cell object regardless of whether it is currently active, disabled, hidden, or being used as a placeholder.

Each visual cell should be represented by a reusable GridCell component. A GridCell should know its row index, column index, displayed value, interaction state, and visual style. Cells should support multiple states including active, disabled, placeholder, selected, highlighted, correct answer, incorrect answer, and header. This allows the same cell prefab to be reused across every game mode without modification.

The GridManager should be responsible for creating and maintaining the board. It should generate all grid cells during initialization, assign row and column coordinates, populate header values, and manage resizing behavior. The GridManager should not contain game-specific logic. Its responsibility is purely visual and structural. It creates the board, maintains references to every cell, and exposes methods that game modes can use to modify cell states and content.

All game-specific functionality should be handled by separate game mode classes. A common GameModeBase parent class should define shared functionality and establish a standard interface for interacting with the grid. Individual modes such as Random Answer Mode, Fill Missing Cells Mode, Row Practice Mode, Column Practice Mode, Factor Finder Mode, and Timed Challenge Mode should inherit from this base class. When a mode is activated, it instructs the GridManager how to configure the cells for that activity.

For example, a "Find the Answer" mode may highlight a multiplication location such as 7 × 8 and ask the player to enter 56. A "Factor Finder" mode may display the value 42 and ask the player to identify which cells produce that result. A "Row Practice" mode may enable only the cells associated with the selected multiplication table while all other cells become placeholders or disabled. A "Column Practice" mode would operate similarly but focus on vertical multiplication sequences. A "Fill the Missing Table" mode may hide selected values throughout the board and require the player to complete the missing entries. Additional game modes can be created later using the same board without modifying the underlying grid system.

The design should prioritize flexibility. The board itself never changes structure. Instead, each game mode changes how the cells behave, what information they display, and how the player interacts with them. This approach creates a strong separation between presentation and gameplay logic, making the project easier to maintain and significantly easier to expand over time.
